doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Learning jazz by doing it and from records
summary: No schools taught jazz; they learned at sessions and by copying 78 rpm records, and Noto was on the road with Kenton while Menza was in the Army.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: He does all right. We’ve heard a lot of different stories about how musicians actually learned the craft of jazz. Some of them that were born in the 20s mostly learned it on the road. Was this something that you guys — how did you learn your craft?

Well by doing it really. I mean you can go and learn all the tunes and the changes and all of that but unless you’re out there doing it — you do sessions all over the place. Free. You play free, but you were learning. And under the right guidance and with a lot of great players, and they would help. And that’s the way I learned, just by doing it. It probably was the same for you.

Absolutely. There were no schools. Academia still really hasn’t accepted jazz as a quote art form, and they really don’t know how to deal with teaching it. I mean there are so many, scores of different approaches to it. And some of them work, some of them don’t. I find the shortcoming — or backtracking — when I learned to play it was learn from records, I had to listen and then I started to copy, I started to— people say well if you think he plays good you ought to listen to this other guy play, and it was always it was a 79¢, 89¢, 99¢ for a ten inch 78 RPM and go out, wear it out and go out and buy another one until you got the solo down.
He’s not as young as he may sound.
Well, slightly younger than Sam. And not much. But in those days, three years was a lot. Or four or five years was a great deal. If you’re 15 and somebody else is 20, that’s a big span there.
It gets closer as you get older.

And by the time I had really started to get to the point where I felt I had some technical and musical prowess, Sam was already out on the road in Stan Kenton’s band and by the time he came back I was in the Army and then I came back again and he was gone, and then he came back to Buffalo and that’s when it all started.
